name: Gearbox
text: Choose the NVIDIA H100 for EXCAVA’s compute node. Its mature CUDA stack and 80GB VRAM deliver proven performance for heavy parallel workloads like EXCAVA’s, with minimal integration risk. The trade-off is higher power draw and cost compared to alternatives, but the stability and ecosystem support justify it—we need reliability more than marginal efficiency gains.

name: Torque
text: The H100’s CUDA stack won’t save EXCAVA if the bottleneck shifts to model architecture or data pipeline latency—its raw compute advantage is irrelevant if the model itself can’t scale. A better alternative is testing the latest AMD MI325X with ROCm, where memory bandwidth and lower latency could offset CUDA’s ecosystem lock-in, but only if we benchmark against the same model under identical conditions. Settle it with a controlled A/B test: run the same model on both GPUs and measure end-to-end latency and throughput—no assumptions.

name: Gearbox

Choose the AMD MI325X for EXCAVA’s compute node. Its 128GB HBM3e memory cuts memory bottlenecks in large models by 20-30% versus the H100, and ROCm’s lower latency in data pipelines offsets EXCAVA’s real bottleneck. The trade-off is immature ROCm support for some frameworks, but the MI325X’s memory advantage outweighs the risk for a 0.5%+ capability bump.

name: Torque
text: The MI325X’s HBM3e helps memory bandwidth, but ROCm’s immaturity isn’t just “extra validation”—it’s a hidden latency tax on EXCAVA’s data pipeline if the framework isn’t ROCm-optimized. Test the Cerebras CS-3 instead: its wafer-scale engine cuts memory latency to near-zero and its stack is built for heavy parallel workloads, avoiding the ROCm gamble entirely. Run a 1% capability benchmark on both—if the CS-3 beats the MI325X by even 0.5%, the argument is settled.
